speaker_role: independent counselor (Nancy Steenson of Steenson College Coaching, interviewed by a college-planning show host)
commercial_incentive: Yes - represents her own college coaching business
key_insights: States the most elite/highly selective schools (Ivies, Stanford, Duke, Boston College cited as examples) do not factor demonstrated interest into decisions, but most other colleges do
Explains 'yield' (percentage of accepted students who enroll) as a metric admissions deans care about and try to protect/increase year over year
Warns that a student can get rejected from a 'safety' school specifically because the college doubts they'll enroll and doesn't want to waste an offer
Notes colleges track digital engagement - whether students open recruitment emails, click links, and how long they spend on the resulting web pages - as a proxy for interest

Recommends students actively engage with virtual tours, admission presentations, roundtables, and social media for schools they're genuinely interested in, especially post-pandemic when in-person visits became less central
States that even strong test scores/grades/recommendations may not overcome a college's perception that a student won't enroll if they show no demonstrated interest
specific_numbers_or_facts: Illustrative hypothetical used by the speaker: a college with 10,000 applications accepting 5,000, with 500 enrolling, yields a 10% yield rate (explicitly framed as a simplified example, not real data)
notable_or_distinctive: Explains the specific mechanism (yield protection and tracked email/website engagement) behind why demonstrated interest affects decisions, rather than just asserting that it matters.
reliability_notes: This is a 2021-era video (COVID-era admissions references) so specifics about virtual outreach may be dated; claims about how colleges track engagement are stated as fact without citing sources; the yield example is explicitly a simplified illustration, not real institutional data.
